parts.title: Booking a room for a party
parts.context: A man phones a community centre to book a room.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man telephoning a community centre to book a room for a party. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Good afternoon, Riverside Community Centre, Karen speaking.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Hello. I'd like to book a room for a party, please. It's for my mother's seventieth birthday.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Oh, lovely. A birthday party. I'll just fill in a booking form, then.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The man wants to book a room for a birthday party, so 'birthday party' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Can I take your name first?

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Yes, it's Mark Harwood.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Could you spell your surname for me?

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Sure. It's H-A-R-W-O-O-D.
script.tts: Sure. It's H, A, R, W, O, O, D.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Thank you, Mr Harwood. And which date were you thinking of?

script.speaker: mark
script.text: It's a Saturday in June. Her actual birthday is on the twentieth, but that's a Friday, and half the family will be working. So we'd like the Saturday after, the twenty-first.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Let me just check the calendar. Yes, Saturday the twenty-first of June is free for most of our rooms. How many guests are you expecting?

script.speaker: mark
script.text: We've sent out forty invitations, but most people are bringing a partner, so I'd say around sixty in total.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Sixty. In that case, the Main Hall would really be too big. It holds two hundred people, so it would feel rather empty. I'd suggest the Garden Room. It takes up to eighty, and it opens straight onto the lawn.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: The Garden Room sounds perfect. My mother loves being outside.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: And what time would you need it?

script.speaker: mark
script.text: The party starts at three, but we'll need an hour before that to put up the decorations. And we should be finished by about half past six.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: There's a wedding reception in the Garden Room that evening, so it has to be empty by seven. So I'll book it for you from two until seven. Is that all right?

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Perfect. We'll be out by then.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Now, the Garden Room has a sound system that you can use for music, and that's included in the price. Is there anything else you'll need?

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Actually, yes. My sister has made a slideshow of old family photos. Could we show that somewhere?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Of course. We can lend you a projector and a screen. There's a charge of twenty pounds for that.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: That's fine. What about food? We're bringing everything ourselves.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: The Garden Room has its own kitchen, with a fridge and an oven. There are cups and glasses, and plenty of knives and forks, but we don't provide plates any more, I'm afraid, because too many got broken. So you'll need to bring your own.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: OK, I'll make a note of that. And is there somewhere for people to park?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Our own car park is quite small, and there's a football match on that Saturday, so it'll be full. But the church next door lets our visitors use its car park, which is just behind the church. It's only a two-minute walk.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: That's good to know. Is there a deposit to pay?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: Yes. The room itself is 35 pounds an hour, which you pay on the day. And we take a deposit, which you get back if everything's left clean and tidy. It used to be 50 pounds, but it went up this year to 75 pounds.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: That's reasonable. And what if something goes wrong on the day, like the heating?

script.speaker: karen
script.text: The office is closed at weekends, so if you have any problems, you should call the caretaker. His phone number is on the door of the Garden Room.

script.speaker: mark
script.text: Great. Thank you very much for your help.

script.speaker: karen
script.text: You're welcome. I'll email you the booking form now.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A library reopens
parts.context: The manager of a public library talks to local residents.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a public library talking to a group of local residents about the library, which has just reopened. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name's Sandra Cole, and I'm the manager of Millbrook Central Library. As you know, the library has been closed for eighteen months, and I'm delighted to say that we reopened last Monday.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: A lot of people have asked me why the work took so long. Many of you assumed it was because of the roof. It's true that the roof leaked, but that was repaired in the first few weeks. The main purpose of the project was to cut our energy bills, which had become enormous. We've added insulation to every wall, replaced all the windows and put solar panels on the roof, and our heating costs have already fallen by half. We didn't make the building any bigger, although moving the offices upstairs has given the public a little more room.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: The whole project cost just over two million pounds. The council paid for about a quarter of that, and several local businesses were very generous too. But most of the money, around sixty per cent, came from a national heritage fund, because this is one of the oldest library buildings in the region.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Now, a word about membership. Joining the library is still free, as it has always been, so nothing changes there. And you'll still need to show us something with your address on it. But you can now fill in the form on our website before you come in, which saves a lot of time at the desk.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: We're also offering some new services. We've run language classes here for many years, and they'll continue as before. What's completely new is our tool library. Instead of buying a drill or a ladder that you'll only use twice a year, you can now borrow tools here, just like books.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Printing from your phone is something many of you have asked for, and we hope to offer it next year, but the system isn't ready yet. We'd also like to stay open later on Sundays, but at the moment we simply don't have enough staff.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: The other new service is for people who find it hard to leave home, because of illness or disability. Volunteers will now deliver books to their door every fortnight, and collect the ones they've finished.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Let me explain where everything is on the ground floor, because it's all changed. Please look at the plan. When you come in through the main entrance, you'll see the reception desk straight away, on your left.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: If you'd like a drink or a snack, our new café is in the corner, just to the left of the reception desk, so it's the first thing you'll come to.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: On your right as you come in are the self-service machines, where you can borrow and return books without queuing. Beyond them is the children's library, which is now twice the size it used to be.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: If you walk straight ahead along the corridor, you'll come to the central hall, which runs across the building from west to east. Turn right into the hall, and on your right, just behind the children's library, you'll find the computer area. There are thirty computers there now, all free to use.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Carry on to the end of the hall, and at the far eastern end there's a large open space. That's where we'll hold exhibitions, and the first one, of old photographs of the town, opens next week.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: If you turn left into the hall instead, the newspapers and magazines are on your left, with some comfortable chairs.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: On the other side of the hall, the north side, is the reading room, which hasn't changed. Right next to it, on its east side, is the local history room, where you can look at old maps and records of the area.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: And finally, the study rooms. There are four of them, and you can book them online for up to three hours at a time. They're also on the north side of the hall, between the local history room and the stairs.

script.speaker: sandra
script.text: Right. Does anyone have any questions?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A project on noise pollution
parts.context: Two students plan a presentation about noise in cities.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students, Priya and Leo, talking about their project on noise pollution in cities. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: So, Priya, we need to finish planning our presentation on noise pollution. But can I ask you something first? Why did you want to do noise? Everyone else chose air quality.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Well, people keep assuming it's because my flat is on the ring road, but honestly, I sleep through the traffic without any problem.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: I thought Dr Mills had suggested it.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: No, she just agreed to it. What got me interested was an article in the newspaper last term, about how long-term noise is linked to heart disease. I had no idea it could affect your health like that.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Well, it was a good choice. Let's talk about our measurements. What surprised you most?

script.speaker: priya
script.text: I expected the shopping street to be the loudest place, and it was, at lunchtime. The station was noisy too, but that was no surprise. What I really didn't expect was the park. With the playground and all the dogs, it was almost as loud as the shopping street.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Yes, that was a shock. And the difference between day and night was much smaller than I thought it would be.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Now, the questionnaire. I've been looking at the replies again. The length was fine. Most people finished it in about five minutes.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: And we got a hundred and twenty replies, which is more than enough.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: True. The real problem was question six. Lots of people misunderstood it, because they didn't know what we meant by ambient noise. We should have explained the term.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: We'll mention that in the presentation, as one of the limitations. So, how should we begin? I was thinking we could start with a definition of noise pollution.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Hmm, that's a bit dull as an opening. Why don't we play the recording we made at the station? Just thirty seconds of it. It would really get people's attention.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Good idea. Let's do that, and give the definition straight afterwards. Then the results.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: The last section is about ways of reducing noise. We looked at six, didn't we? Let's decide what we'll say about each one.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: OK. First, planting trees and hedges along busy roads. They don't reduce noise as much as people think, but I still like them, because birds and insects benefit too.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Yes, I think that's the real advantage.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: Then there are the new quiet road surfaces. Drivers love them, because they're so much smoother. The problem is the price. Replacing the surface of every road would cost far more than most cities can afford.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Next, lower speed limits. Our own council actually tried this on Mill Road last year, and the noise dropped quite a lot.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: We should definitely mention that, since it's local.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: What about better windows? Triple glazing is very effective.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: It is, but it's really hard to fit into older houses, and it's very disruptive. It's mostly used when builders are putting up new flats.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: And then electric buses. In that study we read from Sweden, of all the measures they tested, the electric buses made the biggest difference.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: So we can say that one was the most effective. And finally, quiet hours, where there are rules about noise late at night in residential streets.

script.speaker: priya
script.text: The trouble is, the council can't check every street. It only works if the people living there agree to it and actually follow the rules.

script.speaker: leo
script.text: Right. I think that's our plan done. Shall we start on the slides tomorrow?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the natural ice trade
parts.context: A lecture about the history of the trade in natural ice.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of the trade in natural ice. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Today I want to look at an industry that has almost completely disappeared, but which, for about a hundred years, was surprisingly important: the trade in natural ice. Before electric fridges existed, ice was cut from frozen lakes and rivers in winter, stored, and then sold in the warmer months, and it was even shipped to hot countries on the other side of the world.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The man usually given credit for turning this into a global business is Frederic Tudor, from Boston, in the north-east of the United States. In 1806, Tudor had the idea of selling ice in places where water never froze. So he filled a ship with ice from a frozen pond, and sent it south to the Caribbean. Many people in Boston thought he was mad, and in a way they were right. A lot of the ice melted on the way, and the people who received it had no idea what to do with it. Tudor lost a great deal of money, and within a few years he was deep in debt.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: However, he kept experimenting, and he gradually solved the two main problems: keeping the ice frozen, and creating a demand for it. For insulation, he tried straw, hay and wood shavings, but the material that worked best was sawdust, which the timber mills of New England produced in huge quantities and were happy to give away.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Then, in each port where he sold ice, he built large ice houses. These were buildings with thick double walls, where the ice could be stored for months. And to create demand, he gave away cold drinks, and showed bar owners and restaurants how ice could be used.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The next breakthrough came in the 1820s, when another Boston businessman, Nathaniel Wyeth, invented a plough, pulled by horses, that cut the surface of a frozen lake into a grid. This meant the ice could be harvested in blocks that were all exactly the same size. That might sound like a small detail, but blocks of equal size could be packed tightly together, with very little air between them, so they melted much more slowly, and they were far easier to load onto ships.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: With these improvements, the trade grew rapidly. In 1833, a ship carrying about a hundred and eighty tonnes of ice sailed from Boston to Calcutta, in India. The voyage took four months and crossed the equator twice, but more than half of the ice was still frozen when it arrived.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In the United States itself, the price of ice fell steadily as production grew, and by the middle of the century it was no longer a luxury for the rich. Ordinary families in cities like New York bought ice every day, delivered by the iceman to a wooden icebox in their kitchen.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Ice also changed what people ate. Fishing boats could stay at sea for longer, and trains with ice-cooled wagons carried fish and meat hundreds of kilometres inland, so people far from the coast could buy fresh fish for the first time.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The trade was not limited to America. In Britain, where winters were often too mild to produce thick ice, much of the ice that was used came from Norway. Huge blocks were cut from Norwegian lakes and shipped across the North Sea to ports such as London.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So why did the trade come to an end? There were two main reasons. The first was health. As cities and factories grew, many of the rivers and lakes where ice was harvested became polluted, and doctors began to warn that dirty ice could spread disease. The second reason was technology. Factories that made ice with machines could produce clean ice all year round, close to where it was needed. And from the 1920s onwards, electric refrigerators began to appear in people's homes. By the middle of the twentieth century, the natural ice trade had almost completely disappeared.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: But it left an important legacy. It created the habit of expecting cold drinks and fresh food all year round, and that is exactly the demand that modern refrigeration grew up to meet. Next week, we'll look at how that technology developed.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
